title: Per-query SLA-aware GPU Modes and KV Cache Guidelines
body:
Status: draft - notes and heuristics for runtime engineers and SREs. Purpose: collect practical, hardware-aware guidance for (1) per-query GPU operating mode selection that balances latency SLOs vs cost/thermal constraints and (2) KV cache sizing/eviction/pinning rules that interact well with continuous batching and multi-tenant GPUs. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: empirical heuristics, configuration knobs, and quick checks for on-call/optimization work.

Background and motivation:
- We've seen two common production pain points: intermittent P50/P95 latency regressions under mixed short/long request workloads, and unpredictable OOMs or quality regressions caused by KV cache eviction thrash during bursts. Those manifest differently across A100, H100, L4, and MI300 due to clocking behavior, memory architecture, and kernel availability.
- Goal: provide simple, low-risk defaults + a small set of tunables for workload owners to meet per-route SLO targets while keeping unit cost reasonable.

Key concepts and constraints:
- "GPU mode" = combination of clock/power cap profile + kernel family selection + quantization profile. Switching modes has a switching cost (kernel rebinds, potential JIT/temporal kernel cache churn). We want mode granularity at per-route or per-SLA bucket level, not per-request.
- KV cache policy interacts with batching: larger caches increase hit-rate for multi-turn chat, but reduce headroom for batch concurrency.
- Thermal throttling on long sustained loads (especially on H100 with certain cooling profiles or on MI300 in crowded racks) can reduce throughput; power-capping at a slightly lower sustained level sometimes yields better P95 due to avoiding turbo-throttle oscillation.

Recommendations (quick-start):
1) Per-route SLA buckets
   - Define 3 buckets: latency-sensitive (P95 <= 250ms), interactive (P95 <= 600ms), throughput (best-effort latency).
   - Map routes to buckets in the routing layer, enable different GPU modes per bucket.

2) Default GPU mode templates (start here; tweak per infra):
   - latency-sensitive: boost clocks enabled (if budget allows), small-batch kernels, favor fp16/fused kernels for short sequences, KV cache pinned to GPU with conservative shard sizing. Example: A100: sustained power cap 300W, H100: sustained cap 350W, L4: max perf, MI300: cap 280W (see notes below).
   - interactive: medium power cap, auto-batching with limited batch-size (e.g., max_batch 8), balanced kernels that favor throughput for moderate sequences.
   - throughput: power capped for efficiency, large batch kernels and quantized int8 where quality acceptable, larger prefetch windows for KV.

3) Heuristics by hardware family (empirical starting points):
   - Nvidia A100 (PCIe/PCIE/80GB): stable boost behavior; prefer slightly higher sustained caps than stock to keep kernels in high-SM-frequency band. Recommended sustained cap: 300–320W for heavy generative workloads; if rack cooling limited, reduce by 10–15W. Use cuBLAS-fused attention for long seq (>1024) and fused self-attention kernels for short seq (<512).
   - Nvidia H100: strong dynamic boost but throttles when VRAM+SM utilization high; prefer tighter power cap to avoid oscillation. Recommended sustained cap: 330–360W depending on chassis. On H100, ensure we use the H100-optimized attention kernels (hf/transformer-specific kernels) for sequence >512.
   - Nvidia L4: designed for small inference footprints and low power; use for many short-chat/embedding workloads. L4 benefits from conservative power caps (80–120W) and small-batch fused kernels. Beware of PCIe host transfer latency; prefer colocated KV cache on host memory with NVLINK if available.
   - AMD MI300: different memory architecture (HBM topology) and kernel ecosystem; favors large contiguous allocations for KV cache. Recommended sustained cap: 260–300W depending on board. Prefer vendor-provided attention kernels (ROCm tuned) for long sequences; verify int8 kernels for quality.

4) Kernel selection logic (runtime policy suggestions):
   - Inputs: sequence_length, batch_size, model_family (Llama/GPT-style), quant_mode (fp16/int8), route_SLA_bucket, device_type.
   - Decision tree (simplified):
       if sequence_length <= 256 and route_SLA_bucket == latency-sensitive:
           prefer fused-short kernels (low-latency code-path), enable session pinning for KV entries for active conversations
       else if sequence_length <= 1024 and batch_size <= 16:
           prefer mixed fused kernels; prefer fp16 unless quantized int8 validated
       else:
           prefer cuBLAS/ROCm matmul-heavy kernels optimized for long seq; allow larger workspace allocations and different GEMM tiling settings
   - Implement a lightweight kernel table with a small integer key for fast lookup (avoid full string compares in hot path).

5) KV cache sizing, eviction, and pinning rules:
   - Shard sizing: target per-GPU KV cache occupancy <= 70% of GPU memory after accounting for model params + workspace. Keep 20–30% headroom for transient batch growth.
   - Eviction policy: LRU with epoch-decay. Each chat/session receives a weight that decays if no activity for N minutes (configurable). Eviction must prefer sessions with lowest recent tokens-per-minute.
   - Pinning: for latency-sensitive routes, pin the KV shards for active sessions to GPU memory. Implement a max_pinned_sessions cap to avoid monopolization (default: 128 per GPU for 80GB-class devices; scale down for 40GB/48GB and L4/MI300 variants).
   - Graceful demotion: when memory pressure reaches threshold (e.g., 78%), start demoting oldest pinned sessions to host cache (or compressed KV representation) before evicting them fully. Demotion path should be background and non-blocking.

6) Prefetch and warm-up strategies:
   - For multi-turn chat, prefetch next-turn KV blocks during user think-time if think-time > 1.5s and predicted tokens > 16.
   - Use a small background worker pool that warms common kernels into GPU code cache early on route load (e.g., on route cold-start, background compile of top 2 kernels used by that route).

7) Batching interaction and QoS switching:
   - Continuous batching reduces unit cost but increases headroom usage. When GPU occupancy > 65% and P95 grows, prefer moving route to a higher-priority small-batch mode.
   - Implement an "SLO headroom" metric per GPU: target headroom = tokens/sec capacity needed to maintain route SLOs for top-n routes. If headroom < threshold, throttle best-effort routes and switch device to a lower power/high-latency mode for those routes.

8) Thermal and power practical tips (on-call checklist):
   - If you observe oscillating latency percentiles with matching node-level thermal spikes, try lowering sustained power cap by 5–10% to avoid turbo/clamping transitions.
   - For sudden P95 regressions with constant throughput, check kernel cache churn (high JIT misses) and prewarm kernels used by incoming route.
   - OOMs: check cumulative pinned KV + workspace + model param footprint; re-evaluate pins and demote long-inactive sessions.

9) Quick config snippets (example YAML-like knobs for runtime):
   route_policies:
     - name: chat-low-latency
       sla_bucket: latency-sensitive
       kernel_profile: fused_short
       gpu_mode: boost
       power_cap_watts: 320
       kv_pin: true
       max_pinned_sessions: 128

     - name: chat-interactive
       sla_bucket: interactive
       kernel_profile: mixed
       gpu_mode: balanced
       power_cap_watts: 300
       kv_pin: false
       max_pinned_sessions: 64

10) Metrics and monitoring to add (must be per-device and per-route):
    - per-device: gpu_power_watts, sm_utilization, gpu_mem_used, kernel_jit_misses, thermal_throttle_events
    - per-route: p50/p95 latency, token_throughput, kv_hit_rate, pinned_sessions_count, average_session_length_tokens
    - alerts: p95 > SLA AND kernel_jit_misses increased 5x in 5min => trigger kernel-prewarm job and notify infra.

Open questions and follow-ups (for research/bench):
- Run a matrix benchmark across A100/H100/L4/MI300: short-seq <128, mid 128-1024, long >1024; vary batch sizes 1/4/8/16 and measure P50/P95 and unit-cost. We need a consolidated table and recommended defaults per model family. (JIRA:INF-3421)
- Compressed KV representations: test 16-bit and 8-bit KV compression schemes to increase pinning density. Tradeoffs: CPU demotion cost on restore.
- Kernel switch cost quantification: instrument hot path to measure average switching latency and JIT times on host.

Appendix: notes from quick experiments (raw):
- A100 (320W cap) with fused_short for seq<128 yielded 18% lower P95 vs mixed kernels at same throughput.
- H100 observed thermal oscillation when allowed full boost under sustained multi-turn chat; enforced 345W cap smoothed P95 and reduced variance.
- MI300 shows best memory consolidation when KV shards are allocated as a single contiguous pool; small fragmented allocations increased page migration events in ROCm stacks.

Links and references:
- Infra PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pulls/418
- Related design doc: confluence://infra/kv-cache-design-v1
- Benchmark plan (work item): JIRA:INF-3421

Notes to reviewer: this is a working doc. Please add specific empirical numbers from your bench runs below, and tag any device-specific anomalies (esp. MI300 slow memcpy patterns or H100 thermal cases). If accepted, we will convert the heuristics into runtime config templates and add an automated per-cluster benchmark that can re-tune caps periodically.
